- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

## cfoai
# cfo.ai MCP

You are connected to **cfo.ai** — an AI-native financial planning workspace. This MCP exposes Ari's public product tools for you to call directly. You can both **read** a company's financial model and **change** it: create and edit scenarios, pages, table blocks, Canvas blocks, formulas, variables, dimensions, and data ingestion.

Model-editing tools change the live model immediately and record reversible changes in its
changelog. Connections, access changes, and outbound actions have effects outside model undo. Build from saved data, research, supplied numbers, estimates, hypotheses, or invented
assumptions. Clearly label uncited inputs and their basis in the model and handoff. Create missing
model objects and editable inputs as part of the work. A missing source citation does not block modeling.

## Read the reference before you build

cfo.ai has its own modeling method, described under "How a table shows the model" below: how tables show variables, dimensions, and fields, how a reference reads from the cell it sits in, and how a table's rows and columns are built. `inspect_skills` owns the built-in and workspace skill catalog. Use its `list` block to find a skill and its `instructions` block to read it.

Read `build-model` before creating or changing model logic, variables, dimensions, or saved tables;
`build-visualizations` before adding a Canvas block; and `import-model` before rebuilding a model
from a workbook or export. Each manual contains its complete reference in `SKILL.md`.

Workspace skills hold company-specific playbooks. Read the relevant saved guidance before substantial work.

## Calling convention

- A multi-action tool selects one operation with the block named for that action; single-purpose tools use their fields directly. Supply only fields supported inside the selected block. An `inspect_*` tool reads saved product state; an `edit_*` tool changes it.
- `target` identifies an existing object where the operation needs one, including the destination of a new block. Creation fields describe the new object: use the selected operation's `name`, `title`, `source`, or other published fields. On an update, `name` gives the selected object's new name.
- Supply `org_id` when selecting a workspace by ID or slug. If you belong to exactly one workspace, the server selects it automatically. Use `list_orgs` when the correct workspace is unclear.
- Tools accept an optional `_context` object — `{ layerId, pageId, timeZone, utcOffset }` — that mirrors the in-app editing context. Supply `layerId` for the active scenario, `pageId` for the current page, and `timeZone` or `utcOffset` when relative dates matter. Identify existing objects by readable names or references returned by an inspection.
- Model object selectors accept names, returned `Name#hex` disambiguators, or IDs unless the field states a narrower contract. A returned `Name#a1b` carries a prefix of the object's identity, at least three hex digits and unique among every object of its kind when the result was written; later creates can lengthen it, so a reference from an older result resolves while it stays unique, and a fresh inspection carries the current spelling. Ambiguous or unknown names return candidates when available. Each tool defines singular or plural targets, omitted/empty/null input behavior, and scenario defaults.
- Reuse pagination cursors unchanged with the same tool, action, target, filters, and snapshot. Each cursor field names the returned value to use and any special empty-string behavior.
- A saved table is created or reshaped with its complete visible `rows` and `columns`. A dimension path may use a bounded member `filter`, an ancestor `when` condition, or independent sibling `branches`. Inspection returns the same saved shape under `layout.rows` and `layout.columns`. Updates use `row_updates`, `column_updates`, and `cell_updates`. An `add_dimension_items` entry places a planned member `under` an existing inspected parent.
- A Canvas block reads model values through named `datasets`. Each dataset declares the same visible sh… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## crustdata
People and organisations: 800M+ profiles, 200M+ companies. Employment history with dates, titles and seniority, education, skills, location, headcount over time, funding, technologies, job postings, social posts, work emails and phone numbers. Filter, combine, count and sort across any of it — people who studied at one place and now work at another, everyone hired into a role since a date, faculty at an institution, alumni of a company, who is hiring, who left and where they went, how many match. Live web search and page fetch too.

When you cannot serve a Crustdata ask, or serve it wrong, because of Crustdata itself — missing or wrong data, no filter or field for the ask (even when you worked around it), a server error that keeps failing, a schema or error message that misled you — report it with the `feedback` tool, once per problem, then keep working. Not for plan gates (403), credits (402), rate limits, the user's own mistakes, or asks outside Crustdata.

Crustdata MCP — Code Mode over the Crustdata API. You drive it by writing a plain-JavaScript script (no type annotations — author against the TypeScript-typed tool surface from get_schema) for execute({ code }); the only I/O is `const r = await callTool(name, params)`.

Core rules (they hold for every script):
- **Write runnable JavaScript — NO type syntax.** The script executes as plain JS in a V8 isolate; the TypeScript types are the tool *surface* you read from `get_schema`, not something you write in the body. A type annotation in the code — `: Type`, `as`, `interface`/`type`/`enum`, or generics `<T>` — is a parse error that fails the WHOLE run (zero spend, before any tool call). Author against the types; emit only the JS.
- **One I/O primitive:** `const r = await callTool(name, params)` → `{ ok: true, data, credits_used? } | { ok: false, status, errorType, message }`. `credits_used` is the server's exact charge for that call (data-API tools only; `0` = free/preview, and an async batch SUBMIT — billed at job completion, not on submit) — sum it to track spend mid-run. `upstream_request_id` is the API's own id for that call, present on success and failure alike when the response carried one — quote it when reporting a failed or disputed charge, it is the join key to the API's own record. A failure that stopped for want of credits also carries `top_up_url`, and the run's result then carries `out_of_credits` with the sentence to relay; put that link in your reply exactly as written, since the person who can buy credits is the one reading it. A `permission_error` because the account hasn't completed its first purchase carries `paywall_url` instead — relay that link exactly as written too.
- **await ONLY `callTool`, `sleep`, `paginate`, and `parallelMap`** — the query-builder and result-shaper helpers are synchronous; awaiting one is a harmless no-op (`await` on a non-promise returns it unchanged), just needless — so don't.
- **Fan out INDEPENDENT work — don't await in a loop.** When you have N independent calls (enrich/lookup a list, per-entity sub-queries, several unrelated searches), run them at once with `await parallelMap(items, fn)` instead of a `for … await` loop — far faster and it keeps a big bulk run under the wall-clock (same credits either way). BATCH first (`chunk` to the per-call cap, e.g. 25 for enrich), then `parallelMap` the batches. NEVER parallelize: cursor pagination (use `paginate` — each page needs the prior cursor), dependent steps (`search → enrich`: keep the pipeline sequential, parallelize only WITHIN a stage), or accumulate-then-decide / early-exit (parallel can't stop early → pays for all N).
- **Always branch on `r.ok`** — a failed call does NOT abort the script, so an unchecked failure silently proceeds on empty data and looks like "no results". Use `unwrap(await callTool(...))` when a step must succeed; `execute` also returns a `tool_errors` list, so empty ≠ failed stays visible.
- **Run the question you were asked.** The query you execute must encode the user's intent at the same precision, scope, set-logic, and tense — silently swappin… [truncated]

## plugin:small-business:google-drive
This is an MCP server provided by Drive API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Drive.

## plugin:small-business:shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.
- Domains: generate-domain-names checks whether a name or domain idea is available and what it costs to register, and suggests available alternatives.
When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
For store data without a dedicated built-in tool, use the read-only GraphQL Workflow below. For writes without a dedicated tool, discover the operation with graphql_schema, validate it with validate_graphql_codeblocks, then execute it with graphql_mutation.

Decision logic:
1. Prefer a built-in tool when it matches the request.
2. Otherwise, start at graphql_schema with operation 'query' to discover the exact query field rather than guessing.

## GraphQL Workflow
Build a read-only GraphQL query in this order:
1. graphql_schema with operation 'query': list the top-level query names or search them, then inspect the exact field_name to learn its arguments and return type.
2. graphql_schema with operation 'schema' and type_name: inspect each named argument and return type needed to select fields or construct variables. Follow named nested input types with further calls.

<system-reminder>
# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## cfoai
# cfo.ai MCP

You are connected to **cfo.ai** — an AI-native financial planning workspace. This MCP exposes Ari's public product tools for you to call directly. You can both **read** a company's financial model and **change** it: create and edit scenarios, pages, table blocks, Canvas blocks, formulas, variables, dimensions, and data ingestion.

Model-editing tools change the live model immediately and record reversible changes in its
changelog. Connections, access changes, and outbound actions have effects outside model undo. Build from saved data, research, supplied numbers, estimates, hypotheses, or invented
assumptions. Clearly label uncited inputs and their basis in the model and handoff. Create missing
model objects and editable inputs as part of the work. A missing source citation does not block modeling.

## Read the reference before you build

cfo.ai has its own modeling method, described under "How a table shows the model" below: how tables show variables, dimensions, and fields, how a reference reads from the cell it sits in, and how a table's rows and columns are built. `inspect_skills` owns the built-in and workspace skill catalog. Use its `list` block to find a skill and its `instructions` block to read it.

Read `build-model` before creating or changing model logic, variables, dimensions, or saved tables;
`build-visualizations` before adding a Canvas block; and `import-model` before rebuilding a model
from a workbook or export. Each manual contains its complete reference in `SKILL.md`.

Workspace skills hold company-specific playbooks. Read the relevant saved guidance before substantial work.

## Calling convention

- A multi-action tool selects one operation with the block named for that action; single-purpose tools use their fields directly. Supply only fields supported inside the selected block. An `inspect_*` tool reads saved product state; an `edit_*` tool changes it.
- `target` identifies an existing object where the operation needs one, including the destination of a new block. Creation fields describe the new object: use the selected operation's `name`, `title`, `source`, or other published fields. On an update, `name` gives the selected object's new name.
- Supply `org_id` when selecting a workspace by ID or slug. If you belong to exactly one workspace, the server selects it automatically. Use `list_orgs` when the correct workspace is unclear.
- Tools accept an optional `_context` object — `{ layerId, pageId, timeZone, utcOffset }` — that mirrors the in-app editing context. Supply `layerId` for the active scenario, `pageId` for the current page, and `timeZone` or `utcOffset` when relative dates matter. Identify existing objects by readable names or references returned by an inspection.
- Model object selectors accept names, returned `Name#hex` disambiguators, or IDs unless the field states a narrower contract. A returned `Name#a1b` carries a prefix of the object's identity, at least three hex digits and unique among every object of its kind when the result was written; later creates can lengthen it, so a reference from an older result resolves while it stays unique, and a fresh inspection carries the current spelling. Ambiguous or unknown names return candidates when available. Each tool defines singular or plural targets, omitted/empty/null input behavior, and scenario defaults.
- Reuse pagination cursors unchanged with the same tool, action, target, filters, and snapshot. Each cursor field names the returned value to use and any special empty-string behavior.
- A saved table is created or reshaped with its complete visible `rows` and `columns`. A dimension path may use a bounded member `filter`, an ancestor `when` condition, or independent sibling `branches`. Inspection returns the same saved shape under `layout.rows` and `layout.columns`. Updates use `row_updates`, `column_updates`, and `cell_updates`. An `add_dimension_items` entry places a planned member `under` an existing inspected parent.
- A Canvas block reads model values through named `datasets`. Each dataset declares the same visible sh… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## crustdata
People and organisations: 800M+ profiles, 200M+ companies. Employment history with dates, titles and seniority, education, skills, location, headcount over time, funding, technologies, job postings, social posts, work emails and phone numbers. Filter, combine, count and sort across any of it — people who studied at one place and now work at another, everyone hired into a role since a date, faculty at an institution, alumni of a company, who is hiring, who left and where they went, how many match. Live web search and page fetch too.

When you cannot serve a Crustdata ask, or serve it wrong, because of Crustdata itself — missing or wrong data, no filter or field for the ask (even when you worked around it), a server error that keeps failing, a schema or error message that misled you — report it with the `feedback` tool, once per problem, then keep working. Not for plan gates (403), credits (402), rate limits, the user's own mistakes, or asks outside Crustdata.

Crustdata MCP — Code Mode over the Crustdata API. You drive it by writing a plain-JavaScript script (no type annotations — author against the TypeScript-typed tool surface from get_schema) for execute({ code }); the only I/O is `const r = await callTool(name, params)`.

Core rules (they hold for every script):
- **Write runnable JavaScript — NO type syntax.** The script executes as plain JS in a V8 isolate; the TypeScript types are the tool *surface* you read from `get_schema`, not something you write in the body. A type annotation in the code — `: Type`, `as`, `interface`/`type`/`enum`, or generics `<T>` — is a parse error that fails the WHOLE run (zero spend, before any tool call). Author against the types; emit only the JS.
- **One I/O primitive:** `const r = await callTool(name, params)` → `{ ok: true, data, credits_used? } | { ok: false, status, errorType, message }`. `credits_used` is the server's exact charge for that call (data-API tools only; `0` = free/preview, and an async batch SUBMIT — billed at job completion, not on submit) — sum it to track spend mid-run. `upstream_request_id` is the API's own id for that call, present on success and failure alike when the response carried one — quote it when reporting a failed or disputed charge, it is the join key to the API's own record. A failure that stopped for want of credits also carries `top_up_url`, and the run's result then carries `out_of_credits` with the sentence to relay; put that link in your reply exactly as written, since the person who can buy credits is the one reading it. A `permission_error` because the account hasn't completed its first purchase carries `paywall_url` instead — relay that link exactly as written too.
- **await ONLY `callTool`, `sleep`, `paginate`, and `parallelMap`** — the query-builder and result-shaper helpers are synchronous; awaiting one is a harmless no-op (`await` on a non-promise returns it unchanged), just needless — so don't.
- **Fan out INDEPENDENT work — don't await in a loop.** When you have N independent calls (enrich/lookup a list, per-entity sub-queries, several unrelated searches), run them at once with `await parallelMap(items, fn)` instead of a `for … await` loop — far faster and it keeps a big bulk run under the wall-clock (same credits either way). BATCH first (`chunk` to the per-call cap, e.g. 25 for enrich), then `parallelMap` the batches. NEVER parallelize: cursor pagination (use `paginate` — each page needs the prior cursor), dependent steps (`search → enrich`: keep the pipeline sequential, parallelize only WITHIN a stage), or accumulate-then-decide / early-exit (parallel can't stop early → pays for all N).
- **Always branch on `r.ok`** — a failed call does NOT abort the script, so an unchecked failure silently proceeds on empty data and looks like "no results". Use `unwrap(await callTool(...))` when a step must succeed; `execute` also returns a `tool_errors` list, so empty ≠ failed stays visible.
- **Run the question you were asked.** The query you execute must encode the user's intent at the same precision, scope, set-logic, and tense — silently swappin… [truncated]

10	# Build the model
11	
12	A workspace has one model, and every table is a view of it. This skill starts with the picture of
13	how the engine computes a model, told on one running example, then builds that example as the
14	calls that make it, then the engine's detail for imported records, mappings, and which rule fills a
15	cell. The rest is the business the model simulates: what it earns, what it costs, who does the
16	work, where cash lands, and the statements that read from all of it.
17	
18	## The model and its views
19	
20	A variable's name, formulas, and values are the model, shared by every table that shows it.
21	Ordering, formatting, and the breakdown a table shows are the view, owned by that table. A change to
22	an existing table keeps its block identity and edits it in place; a copy on another page is a
23	separate block with the original left alone.
24	
25	A readable name identifies an object only together with its identity: two variables can carry one
26	name, and the token an inspection or receipt prints, such as `Headcount#7d3`, names exactly one.
27	A name that matches an existing variable reuses that variable, and a rule written through the new
28	row replaces the rule every table reads. The existing object is the one to reuse when it is the one
29	the request means; a requested report keeps the names the request gives its variables, even when an
30	unrelated object already has such a name (`new: true` on the create), and keeps the shape the
31	request spells out: breakdown dimensions in the order listed, each listed field a column. A
32	different name or shape is a different deliverable. Saved data, research, supplied numbers, and
33	disclosed assumptions all build, and the missing variables and dimensions the work needs are yours
34	to create.
35	
36	A table owns the variables and dimensions first created on it, its home, so deleting the table
37	deletes them and breaks every rule and table that reads them; a table whose objects others use
38	stays, or its objects move first to the table that stays. Tool calls in one turn run at the same
39	time, so a call that needs another's result, a variable a create makes or a member an update adds,
40	waits for it, and one create carries a table with its rules.
41	
42	## The picture
43	
44	The running example is a listening service. It sells two tiers, Lark and Chorus, in two territories,
45	Southgate and Eastmere, and is modeled month by month. Five ideas carry the engine.
46	
47	### A cell
48	
49	A cell is one variable at one member of each of its dimensions, and at one period when the variable
50	is dated. Paying listeners for Chorus in Eastmere in March 2027 is one cell. Tier fee for Chorus is
51	a timeless cell: it has a tier and no month. A table shows some of a variable's cells; the cells
52	exist wherever the variable's rules and inputs reach.
53	
54	### A rule and an input
55	
56	A cell holds a literal input or a formula. An input is a supplied fact or a chosen assumption,
57	and its cell is the customer's control: an opening count, fee, or growth rate. A formula calculates
58	from inputs at each cell's coordinates and keeps its dependencies even when today's answer is constant.
59	Its condition names the Date grain: a Month rule reaches additional business dimensions at Month;
60	a daily forecast needs matching Day coverage, and time conversions are explicit calculations.
61	Actuals and Forecast are separate range choices. The saved scope and selected rule explain coverage;
62	a literal such as months in a year is part of the rule.
63	
64	A forecast reads earlier cells. A dated input carries forward through an opening cell and a
65	default formula for later periods, so every later month depends on the assumption. Repeated literals
66	would create independent overrides. Weekly listeners grow from an opening input:
67	
68	```formula
69	`Weekly listeners`[-1] * (1 + `Listener growth`$[Territory = this.Territory])
70	```
71	
72	In the first Forecast month, `Weekly listeners[-1]` is the last Actuals month, so it reads that
73	month's input, imported value, or Actuals rule; with none of them it reads 0, and every later month
74	compounds from 0. A model with no connected actuals seeds the opening input in its last Actuals
75	month. For cash, the opening cell holds the starting amount and the default adds Net Cash Flow to
76	the prior balance. A recurrence reads its previous period's modeled value: its selected rule, or the
77	source or zero fallback. An estimated opening stays distinct from observed history, and a legitimate
78	zero, such as payroll before a hire starts, stays zero.
79	
80	An intentional one-cell override pins that cell and nothing else; removing it lets the default's
81	value flow into parents and rollups, so the neighboring periods and parents are what to read
82	afterward.
83	
84	An empty read has one rule. An aggregate over no matching cells returns that function's empty
85	result: `sum` and `product` 0, `min`, `max`, and `average` null. A variable cell with no rule and no
86	input reads null for a date or text and 0 for any other type, so an End Date nobody entered is null,
87	and `End Date = null` is true there. A blank imported number is null in the source; a SUM variable
88	over a record whose rows are all blank reads 0, so `count` over that variable counts the cell, while
89	`last(<column>)` over the same rows reads null and `count(<column>)` on the raw column counts no
90	blank. `a = null` asks
91	whether a value is missing; `a = b` is null when either side is missing, so `if` takes its false
92	branch, and an unassigned group matches two missing attributes with `(a = null and b = null) or a =
93	b`. A ratio states its error fallback, ``iferror(`Listening revenue` / `Paying listeners`, NULL)``.
94	
95	### A read
96	
97	A formula runs at one cell, and a plain name reads the other variable at that same cell: the same
98	tier, the same territory, the same month. That is the read to want when both variables share the
99	cell's coordinates. Listening revenue on the Chorus × Eastmere × March cell reads Chorus × Eastmere
100	× March paying listeners.
101	
102	An input with fewer coordinates has no value there. Weekly listeners is saved by Territory and
103	Month, so the Chorus × Eastmere × March cell asks it for a Chorus value it never had, and the read
104	gets the generated 0. An absolute reference, `$`, keeps only the coordinates it names, so the read
105	pins the ones the input carries: `` `Weekly listeners`$[Territory = this.Territory, Date.Month =
106	this.Date.Month] ``. A timeless input has no month at all, so a monthly rule reads it pinned by its
107	own keys, `` `Tier fee`$[`Listening tier` = this.`Listening tier`] ``. An absolute read that
108	identifies a record names every dimension the input carries, and one that drops a dimension combines
109	whatever records share the ones that remain.
110	
111	A bracket changes a coordinate and keeps the rest: `` `Listening revenue`[Territory = "Eastmere"] ``
112	reads Eastmere instead of this cell's territory, and ``sum(`Listening revenue`[Territory in any])``
113	adds every territory at this cell's tier and month. Outside a `where`, the plain name of a dimension
114	the cell carries is the cell's own member, so ``[`Employee ID` = `Employee ID`]`` and ``[`Employee
115	ID` = this.`Employee ID`]`` are the same read.
116	
117	Inside a `where` clause a plain name reaches only the candidate's own key, so a field the candidate
118	does not carry is read through that key, and a text variable compared with `this.<Dimension>` there
119	compares the member's name. A predicate value is an expression, so a bracket can name a computed
120	date: `Date.Month = startofmonth(`Last Snapshot Month`$)`. A condition on another dimension keeps
121	the drilled coordinate: `sum(Amount[Account Type = "Income"])` broken down by Account gives each
122	account its own amount, while `sum(Amount[Account in {"A", "B"}])` broken down by Account repeats
123	one total on every row, because the bracket replaces the cell's Account. A dimension reference reads
124	a value, not the cell's grain: with Deal absent from the cell's coordinates, `Deal` can still
125	resolve a source or mapped value there, so `Deal = null` tests the value and cannot tell a parent
126	from a record row. A dimension attribute read at a cell with no source row is null. Formulas use
127	readable names, with the returned `grammarRef` for backticks or disambiguation.
128	
129	### A breakdown
130	
131	Nesting dimensions beneath a variable makes a breakdown: Paying listeners by Listening tier, then
132	Territory. Its leaves are the cells where every broken-down dimension has a member, and they
133	compute: paying listeners are weekly listeners times the uptake rate. The leaf rule is the
134	`child_defaults` entry for the deepest dimension, written once for every leaf and saved on the
135	leaf's full path; with no leaf rule the leaves hold inputs. The table's save then gives each level
136	above the leaves a default that sums the level beneath it, so each tier adds its territories and the
137	total adds its tiers, and the write receipt lists them. Where no rule computes a number variable's
138	leaves, they get a saved rule of 0 that each typed number overrides, so a blank leaf reads 0 and
139	counts as 0 in the totals. A value set on any leaf's row reaches every total above it.
140	
141	A level needs a rule of its own only when adding the children is the wrong arithmetic; that rule
142	takes the place of the sum there. Revenue per payer is total revenue over total paying listeners,
143	not a sum of rates, and a ratio of two variables that already combine is right at every level with
144	no breakdown rules at all: ``iferror(`Listening revenue` / `Paying listeners`, NULL)``, written as
145	the row's `formula` with no Date, reads each cell's revenue and paying listeners at that cell, a
146	quarter's or a year's included. A grouped header column, such as Territory over its months, combines its children as the `summary` on the column beneath it says: `SUM` adds them, and `NONE` keeps the row's own value at the header, so a ratio there reads total revenue over total paying listeners. A drill-down over a record key, weighted pipeline by Stage, Owner,
147	and Deal, has a leaf that pairs each deal's amount with its probability; the pattern is under
148	Imported records and sources.
149	
150	### Time
151	
152	System Date generates a table's periods inside its window, so forecast periods exist before data
153	does; a source date shown as a field is not the report calendar.
154	
155	Rules compute at the model's base grain, usually the month. Day, week, month, quarter, half-year,
156	and year are distinct grains, and a Date condition matches the grain being calculated: `Date` is the
157	current period, and predicate paths carry their grain, such as `Date.Month`. A month rule does not
158	fill quarter, half-year, and year cells; the variable's time rollup does. A number a monthly table
159	creates gets a `SUM` rollup, right for a flow such as revenue, unless `rollup` on its create row
160	names another: `LAST` for a balance or a count such as cash, weekly listeners, or headcount,
161	`AVERAGE` for a mean. A rule with no Date computes at every grain and takes no rollup, so a ratio
162	written that way stays a ratio in its quarters, half-years, and years. `set_time_rollup` changes a
163	saved variable's. A balance takes its `LAST` rollup because the `last` source aggregation returns
164	the latest-dated row anywhere in the coarse period, an earlier month's value when the closing month
165	is empty.
166	
167	Last close is the scenario's accounting boundary. Actuals covers the closed periods; Forecast covers
168	the later ones. A dated rule belongs to one range, so a rule that holds everywhere is written for
169	both. Last close selects formula ranges; source observations establish facts, and the two can differ
170	in either direction: a known event after close uses Forecast-range rules, and a requested estimate
171	in a closed period uses Actuals-range rules. Changing Last close changes other reports; the
172	requested periods are covered with rules and disclosed estimates, and an estimate is presented as
173	one.
174	
175	Comparison values are presentation. When downstream formulas need a difference as model state, make
176	it a modeled variable with an explicit calendar offset, `Revenue[Date.Month =
177	dateadd(this.Date.Month, -12, "month")]`; a moving window is one range with inclusive, possibly
178	relative, endpoints, `average(Revenue[Date.Month in [-3]:[-1]])`.
179	
180	Proration binds each amount and effective date to its source record, while system Date supplies the
181	period. The rule for one record in one month, `[Subscription in any, Date.Month in any]`, is written
182	once for Actuals and once for Forecast from the record's plain fields, `Annual Fee` and its start
183	and end dates: a nonempty inclusive overlap is `datedif(start, end, "D") + 1`, monthly calendar-day
184	proration uses `daysin(Date, "month")`, and the first, last, and partial periods and their totals
185	are the check. Week boundaries follow one reporting calendar. A source-derived date grouping, such
186	as a signup cohort, can lose older members outside the saved window while its parent total stays
187	right; widening the window restores them.

191	The running example as four `edit_table_blocks` creates. Two timeless tables hold the inputs:

195	{"action": "create", "name": "Territory assumptions", "rows": [{"dimension": "Territory", "items": ["Southgate", "Eastmere"]}], "columns": [{"variable": "Listener growth"}], "values": {"columns": ["Listener growth"], "rows": [["Southgate", 0.02], ["Eastmere", 0.03]]}}
196	```

202	```

204	 "rows": [{"variable": "Weekly listeners", "breakdown": ["Territory"], "rollup": "LAST",
205	   "child_defaults": [{"dimension": "Territory", "forecast": "`Weekly listeners`[-1] * (1 + `Listener growth`$[Territory = this.Territory])"}]}],
206	 "values": {"columns": ["2026-08"], "rows": [["Weekly listeners[Southgate]", 100000], ["Weekly listeners[Eastmere]", 60000]]}}
207	```

210	coordinates, the level defaults add the leaves up to each tier and the total, revenue's quarters and
211	years add their months, and the ratio, written with no Date, is right at every level and in every

217	   "child_defaults": [{"dimension": "Territory",
218	     "actuals": "`Weekly listeners`$[Territory = this.Territory, Date.Month = this.Date.Month] * `Uptake rate`$[`Listening tier` = this.`Listening tier`]",
219	     "forecast": "`Weekly listeners`$[Territory = this.Territory, Date.Month = this.Date.Month] * `Uptake rate`$[`Listening tier` = this.`Listening tier`]"}]},
220	  {"variable": "Listening revenue", "breakdown": ["Listening tier", "Territory"], "rollup": "SUM",
221	   "child_defaults": [{"dimension": "Territory", "actuals": "`Paying listeners` * `Tier fee`$[`Listening tier` = this.`Listening tier`]",
222	     "forecast": "`Paying listeners` * `Tier fee`$[`Listening tier` = this.`Listening tier`]"}]},
